summary: Describes extensions to OSPF so routers can forward IP multicast datagrams, building delivery trees from the link-state database OSPF already maintains. It was written as a standards-track proposal. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: MOSPF adds multicast forwarding to OSPF by recording where group members are. Routers use that information to send copies of a message along paths that reach those members.

questions: how does multicast work in ospf
how does multicast routing work in ospf
what is a wild-card multicast receiver
subtitle: OSPF extensions that build source-based delivery trees for multicast groups.

tldr.problem: OSPF's unicast routes do not by themselves tell routers where members of an IP multicast group are located.
tldr.mechanism: MOSPF adds group-membership link state advertisements. Routers use them with the OSPF topology map to build a shortest-path tree from each multicast source and prune branches without group members.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1584 is Historic. Its design allowed multicast-capable and ordinary OSPF routers to coexist for unicast, but ordinary routers do not forward multicast.

today: RFC 1584 is marked Historic in the unit metadata. It was published in March 1994, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Multicast Routing in OSPF
sections.content:
RFC 1584 defines MOSPF, backward-compatible extensions to Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) Version 2 for forwarding IP multicast datagrams. Multicast hosts join groups using the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP), while MOSPF routers use OSPF's link-state database to learn the network topology.

A new group-membership link state advertisement (LSA) identifies routers and transit networks with group members. The router calculates a tree from the datagram's source and destination group, then caches the forwarding result for later packets.
sections.plainLanguage: MOSPF adds information about group membership to the network map OSPF routers already share. That lets routers calculate where multicast packets should go.

sections.title: Build and Prune a Delivery Tree
sections.content:
MOSPF routes using both the source and multicast destination. It builds a shortest-path tree from the source using OSPF link costs, then removes branches that do not lead to a router or transit network labeled for the group.

A forwarding-cache entry records the upstream neighbor and downstream interfaces for a source and group. Routers build the tree when the first matching datagram arrives. A topology change clears the forwarding cache; a change to a group's membership clears entries for that group.
sections.plainLanguage: For each source and group, a router finds the shortest paths to places with members. It removes unused branches and keeps the forwarding result for later packets.

sections.title: Areas and Group-Membership LSAs
sections.content:
Group-membership LSAs are flooded within one OSPF area. Inter-area multicast forwarders summarize membership from non-backbone areas into the backbone, where the combined information can guide delivery across areas.

Those forwarders act as wild-card multicast receivers in non-backbone areas, receiving traffic regardless of its group. The LSA is Type 6 and lists transit vertices to label for a group. The OSPF Options field's MC bit indicates multicast capability; the router-LSA's W bit marks a wild-card receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Each area shares its own group list, and designated forwarders carry summaries into the backbone. A Type 6 LSA names the group and the network locations that have members.

sections.title: Mixed Routers and Security
sections.content:
MOSPF routers can coexist with routers that implement only ordinary OSPF, and both can forward unicast traffic. Ordinary OSPF routers do not forward multicast, and MOSPF does not define a tunnel for carrying multicast through them.

The Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It does not describe added authentication or protection for the group-membership information.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary OSPF routers can still carry unicast traffic alongside MOSPF routers. They cannot carry multicast traffic, and the RFC does not discuss security protections.
